question: Why is a walk with someone else often easier than the same walk alone?
options: Company makes the effort feel smaller than it is
Two people always walk faster than one
Talking makes your muscles work less hard
Walking together uses a different set of muscles
explanation: Effort has a felt size as well as a real one, and company shrinks the felt one. The walk is the same distance; it just costs you less attention.

review.notes: Guessable by elimination: the three distractors are all physiological absurdities ('talking makes your muscles work less hard', 'walking together uses a different set of muscles', 'two people always walk faster than one' — note the giveaway 'always'), so the correct option is the only one that is even about how effort feels. Replace at least two distractors with plausible psychological mechanisms (e.g. 'you stop keeping track of how far you have gone', 'you set off before you can talk yourself out of it') so the reader has to know which one is right.

question: What usually happens when a household starts moving at the same time each day?
options: Everyone gets the same amount of benefit from it
The time itself starts doing the remembering for you
It only works if everyone does the same activity
The youngest person sets the pace for everybody
explanation: A habit attached to a time of day stops needing a decision. Nobody has to propose it, which is the part that usually fails.

review.notes: Distractor quality. 'Everyone gets the same amount of benefit from it' is plainly false, 'It only works if everyone does the same activity' is defeated by its own 'only', and 'The youngest person sets the pace' is unrelated to the question asked. The correct option is also the only figuratively phrased one, which makes it stand out visually. Also overlaps heavily with SF-TRV-000320, which teaches the same time-anchoring point in the same slice — keep one.

question: A grandparent and a child go for the same walk. Who is getting a real workout?
options: Only the child, because they move faster
Only the grandparent, because it is harder for them
Both, because effort is measured against your own body
Neither — a walk is too gentle to count for either
explanation: Effort is relative to the person doing it. The same pace can be easy for one body and genuinely demanding for another, and both count.

review.notes: Textbook answer-shape giveaway: the options are 'Only A', 'Only B', 'Both', 'Neither', and 'Both' is the correct one. In an app whose whole voice is that everyone's effort counts, a nine-year-old will pick it without knowing anything about relative effort. The teaching point is good — keep it, but rewrite the options so the inclusive answer is not the only kind one (e.g. make a distractor 'Both, but only once they are out of breath', which is also inclusive and still wrong).

question: Why do people often keep a habit longer when somebody else knows about it?
options: Being watched makes your body work more efficiently
Other people remind you more often than you remember
It turns the habit into a competition you want to win
The habit becomes something shared rather than private
explanation: Once somebody else knows, skipping it is a small thing you would be doing to them too. That is different from a promise you made only to yourself.

review.notes: Two defensible answers. Option 1, 'Other people remind you more often than you remember', is a real and well-documented mechanism for why shared habits stick, so marking it wrong makes the item feel arbitrary. Either make that distractor clearly inadequate or rewrite the stem to ask specifically why it holds up even when nobody reminds you. Separately, the explanation ('skipping it is a small thing you would be doing to them too') leans on obligation to others in a way that sits awkwardly against the app's no-shame rule — consider framing it as shared rather than owed.

question: What is the most useful thing to say to someone coming back after a long gap?
options: Tell them the gap barely matters now that they are back
Ask what stopped them so it does not happen again
Remind them how well they were doing before
Say nothing about the gap and get straight on with it
explanation: The gap is the thing they are already thinking about. Naming it lightly and moving on beats both silence and a post-mortem.

review.notes: A judgement call presented as having one right answer. 'Say nothing about the gap and get straight on with it' and 'Remind them how well they were doing before' are both things thoughtful people genuinely do, and the explanation asserts the chosen option 'beats both silence and a post-mortem' without any basis offered. `editorial` confidence is fine for an opinion, but a trivia item marks three defensible choices as errors. Either reframe as a Rickie aside rather than a quiz, or make the distractors things that are actually unhelpful (e.g. 'Ask them to promise it will not happen again').

question: Two people start the same routine on the same day. A month later one has gone further. What does that most likely mean?
options: One of them tried considerably harder
Bodies respond to the same work at different rates
The other one was doing the movements incorrectly
The first one has better natural ability for it
explanation: Response to the same training varies a lot between people and always has. It says very little about how hard either one worked.

review.notes: True (inter-individual variability in training response is well documented), safe, non-comparative, and all four options are beliefs people actually hold. The explanation adds information rather than restating the option.

question: Why does doing something active with a child tend to work better than telling them to?
options: Adults are better at explaining while they move
It guarantees the child is doing it correctly
Children copy what they see far more than what they hear
Children need supervision for most kinds of movement
explanation: Watching somebody do a thing ordinarily is the most reliable teaching there is. It also removes the part where it sounds like an instruction.

review.notes: Firmness: 'Watching somebody do a thing ordinarily is the most reliable teaching there is' is a superlative the evidence does not support — parental modelling is associated with children's activity, it is not established as the single most reliable form of teaching. Soften to something like 'is a large part of how children learn'. Also two of the distractors ('It guarantees the child is doing it correctly', 'Children need supervision for most kinds of movement') do not answer the question asked, which narrows the field to two before the reader thinks.

question: What tends to happen to a shared activity when one person is much better at it?
options: It motivates the other person to catch up quickly
It has no effect as long as nobody mentions it
The stronger person gets a poorer workout from it
The gap makes it feel like a test
explanation: Difficulty that is obviously mismatched stops being company and starts being assessment. Picking something you are both mediocre at works better.

review.notes: States one side of a genuinely mixed picture as fact. A visibly stronger partner can also raise effort and motivation (the Köhler effect is well replicated), so 'It motivates the other person to catch up' is not simply wrong, and 'The stronger person gets a poorer workout from it' is often true as well. The stem says 'tends to happen', which claims a direction the literature does not settle. Mark `contested` and say so in the text, or narrow the stem to the specific case the explanation is really about (a mismatch neither person can ignore).

question: Why is walking a dog unusually good at keeping people consistent?
options: The obligation cannot be rescheduled
Dogs need more exercise than people do
It makes the walk longer than you would choose
Walking a dog uses more effort than walking alone
explanation: The dog will not accept 'tomorrow'. An external obligation you cannot renegotiate is a far stronger commitment than an internal one.

review.notes: Only one option is on topic. The question asks about consistency; three of the four options are about distance or effort, so the reader can select the right answer purely by matching subject matter without knowing anything about dogs or commitment. Rewrite the distractors as competing explanations for consistency (e.g. 'the dog is pleased to see you go', 'the walk happens at the same time each day').

question: What makes a household routine survive one person losing interest?
options: Having a rule about what happens if somebody stops
The routine belonging to the day, not a person
Making sure nobody notices that they stopped
Choosing an activity that person was never keen on
explanation: If the routine only exists because one person drives it, it ends when they do. Attached to a time instead, it survives anyone's off week.

review.notes: Two throwaway distractors — 'Making sure nobody notices that they stopped' and 'Choosing an activity that person was never keen on' are not things anyone would propose — leaving one real alternative. It is also a near-duplicate of SF-TRV-000312: both items' correct answer is 'anchor the routine to a time, not a person'. Cut one of the two or give this one a distinct angle.

question: Why is it worth letting a younger person choose the activity sometimes?
options: Their choice will usually be more physically demanding
It is the only way to know what they enjoy
Choosing it makes them far more likely to turn up for it
Adults tend to pick activities that are too difficult
explanation: Having chosen a thing changes your relationship to it. The activity matters much less than whose idea it was.

review.notes: Overstated for a `simplified` item with no source. Choice and autonomy do improve adherence, but 'far more likely to turn up' and 'The activity matters much less than whose idea it was' are much firmer than the evidence, which shows a modest effect. Soften to 'more likely', drop the second sentence's comparative claim, or cite a self-determination-theory source and promote to `established`.

question: What is the effect of turning a shared walk into a daily step target?
options: It reliably makes everybody walk further
It helps most when the people walk at different speeds
Targets work better for groups than for individuals
It can turn company into something you can fail at
explanation: A number introduces the possibility of falling short. That is sometimes useful and sometimes the thing that ends a walk people were enjoying.

review.notes: Well hedged ('can turn', 'sometimes useful and sometimes'), teaches a real and non-obvious idea, and the explanation gives both sides rather than restating the option. Distractor 'Targets work better for groups than for individuals' is genuinely tempting.

question: Somebody in the house says they are too tired to join. What generally helps most?
options: Offering a much shorter version of the same thing
Encouraging them to push through it anyway
Leaving them out and not mentioning it again
Asking them to commit to tomorrow instead
explanation: A shorter version keeps the habit and the company intact without arguing about whether the tiredness is real. It usually is.

review.notes: No option in the set respects a stated 'no'. Someone says they are too tired; 'Leaving them out and not mentioning it again' and 'Asking them to commit to tomorrow instead' are both marked wrong, so the only sanctioned response is to counter-offer a smaller ask. The explanation concedes the tiredness 'usually is' real and still recommends negotiating past it. In an app used by children, this teaches mild social pressure on a family member's stated limit, and it sits badly against the product's own anti-pressure framing. Needs either an option that simply accepts the no, or a stem that asks what keeps the invitation open rather than what 'helps most'.

question: Why do people often move more on holiday without noticing?
options: Warmer places make movement feel easier
The movement is attached to something you want to do
Holidays generally involve more planned exercise
People have more energy when they are rested
explanation: Walking to see something is not experienced as exercise at all. The same distance on a treadmill is a task; here it is the way you got there.

review.notes: Soft, hedged ('often'), harmless, and teaches a real framing effect. 'Without noticing' in the stem does enough work to separate it from the 'more energy when rested' distractor.

question: What happens to your sense of balance as you get older, if nothing is done about it?
options: It stays the same but your legs get weaker
It improves as you get more practice at it
It gradually fades, and practicing it slows that down
It changes only after a fall has already happened
explanation: Balance behaves like a skill rather than a fixed trait: unused it fades, practiced it holds up remarkably well.

review.notes: The stem telegraphs the answer. 'if nothing is done about it' signals that the right option is the one mentioning what happens when something IS done, and only option 2 does — it is also the longest. The underlying claim is sound, so this is purely an options fix: drop the qualifier from the stem, or move 'practicing it slows that down' into the explanation and make the options compete on what actually happens to balance.

question: Can somebody in their eighties still build strength?
options: No, muscle stops responding after about sixty
Only if they were strong when they were younger
Only with equipment designed for older people
Yes, muscle responds to being used at any age
explanation: Studies in people well into their nineties have found real strength gains. The rate is slower; the response itself does not switch off.

review.notes: THE CITATION IS WRONG. This is the only `established` item in the slice and its sole source, PMID 2360822, is 'Pentoxifylline modulates meningeal inflammation in experimental bacterial meningitis' (Antimicrob Agents Chemother, 1990) — nothing to do with strength training. The paper the explanation is describing is Fiatarone et al., 'High-intensity strength training in nonagenarians', JAMA 1990, which is PMID 2342214. The claim is true and the item is otherwise good; swap the source to https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2342214/ and re-check every other `established` citation in this batch, because the validator only checks that `sources` is non-empty, not that the URL resolves to the right paper.

question: Why do teenagers sometimes get clumsier for a while?
options: Limbs change length faster than coordination updates
They are growing tired faster than they realize
Their balance organs are still finishing developing
Growth makes muscles temporarily weaker
explanation: Your brain holds a map of how long your arms and legs are. During a growth spurt the map is briefly out of date, and coordination catches up after.

review.notes: Stated far more firmly than the evidence supports. 'Adolescent awkwardness' is poorly supported and actively disputed: a systematic review of sensorimotor function in adolescence found inconsistent results, several longitudinal studies aligned on peak height velocity found no decline (strength, speed and flexibility rose through the growth spurt), and a 2025 narrative review concludes there is no consensus definition and limited empirical evidence for the phenomenon at all. The 'brain holds an out-of-date map of your limb length' mechanism is a popular explanation, not an established one. Either mark `contested` and say in the text that it is argued over, or cut the item. Do not ship it as `simplified` fact to teenagers who will read it as a description of themselves.

question: What is the main reason older adults are encouraged to keep doing strength work?
options: It is the fastest way to improve heart health
It keeps everyday independence
It is gentler on joints than walking is
It replaces the need for balance practice
explanation: The point is rarely the muscle itself. It is getting out of a chair unaided and carrying your own shopping, which is what strength buys you later.

review.notes: True and well supported, and the explanation earns its place by naming what independence concretely means (getting out of a chair, carrying shopping) rather than restating the option. Minor: 'It keeps everyday independence' reads slightly clipped.

question: Do children need to train the way adults do to get benefit from moving?
options: Yes, structure matters more for children than adults
Children only benefit from organized sport
No — varied play covers most of what they need
Children need shorter but much harder sessions
explanation: Climbing, chasing and messing about covers strength, balance, coordination and stamina at once, which is roughly what a structured program is for.

review.notes: Formatting tell — the correct option is the only one beginning 'No —' and the only one containing a dash, so it is visually distinct before it is read. Combined with 'Children only benefit from organized sport', which its own 'only' defeats, the field collapses to two. Rephrase the correct option to match the others' shape and make the sport distractor plausible (e.g. 'Organised sport covers it more completely than play does').

question: What happens to reaction time as people age?
options: It is fixed from birth and never changes
It slows sharply and suddenly in your sixties
It improves with age because of experience
It slows a little, less so in active people
explanation: Some slowing is ordinary. How much is heavily influenced by whether you keep doing things that demand a quick response.

review.notes: The correct option is conspicuously the only hedged, two-clause, nuanced one, which is the standard tell — readers learn to pick the careful-sounding answer. 'It is fixed from birth and never changes' is also a throwaway nobody would choose. Additionally, 'less so in active people' is largely cross-sectional evidence and is stated here as settled causation; soften to something like 'and people who keep doing quick-response things tend to slow less', or source it.

question: Why does recovery from a hard effort tend to take longer as you get older?
options: Several repair processes each run a little slower
Muscles become permanently more fragile
Older people work harder for the same result
The body stops repairing muscle after middle age
explanation: No single system fails; a number of them just run at a slightly reduced pace. The practical answer is more time between hard efforts, not fewer.

review.notes: The question's premise is not established and recent evidence points the other way. A 2025 systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression found advancing age is NOT associated with greater exercise-induced muscle damage, and that older adults reported substantially less soreness at 48 and 72 hours than younger ones; a 2023 scoping review on recovery from resistance exercise in older adults concluded the findings are too inconsistent to support clear recommendations. This item asserts 'recovery tends to take longer as you get older' in the stem as settled fact and then gives training advice built on it. Rewrite the stem so it does not presuppose the effect, mark `contested`, and say in the text that it is argued over — or cut the item. Two of the distractors ('Muscles become permanently more fragile', 'The body stops repairing muscle after middle age') are throwaways regardless.

question: At what age is it too late to start being active?
options: Around seventy, when injury risk becomes too high
There is no age at which starting stops helping
Once you have been inactive for over a decade
It depends entirely on your family history
explanation: People who begin late still measurably improve. Starting is worth more than the age at which you start.

review.notes: The claim is true, but the item is unguessable-proof in the wrong direction: 'There is no age at which starting stops helping' is the answer this app always gives, and 'It depends entirely on your family history' is defeated by its own 'entirely'. It is also redundant with SF-TRV-000326 in the same slice, which already makes the never-too-late point with better distractors and an actual study behind it. Cut this one or give it a specific, checkable payload (what late starters actually gain, and how fast).

question: Why do bones need to be loaded to stay strong?
options: Loading warms the bone and helps it grow
Pressure forces minerals into the bone from the blood
Bone rebuilds itself in response to being used
Loading stretches bone slightly, making it longer
explanation: Bone is living tissue that constantly rebuilds. Regular load is the signal telling it how strong it needs to be.

review.notes: Mechanism question that genuinely requires knowing the answer, and 'Pressure forces minerals into the bone from the blood' is a properly tempting distractor. Claim (bone remodels in response to mechanical load) is solidly established and the explanation explains rather than restates.

question: What does 'use it or lose it' actually describe in the body?
options: A rule that applies only to muscle tissue
The idea that rest is always harmful
A gradual loss that begins at a fixed age
Tissue kept in proportion to its demand
explanation: Muscle, bone and balance are all maintained at roughly the level demanded of them. Reduce the demand and the body economizes.

review.notes: The correct option is the grammatical odd one out: three options open 'A rule... / The idea... / A gradual loss...' and the fourth opens 'Tissue kept...', so it can be picked on shape alone. 'The idea that rest is always harmful' is also a throwaway. Separately, 'Tissue kept in proportion to its demand' is abstract phrasing for a stated min_age of 9 — the explanation is clearer than the option it explains, which suggests the option should be rewritten in the explanation's language.

question: Is stiffness in the morning a normal part of getting older?
options: Yes, and moving gently usually eases it
No, it always indicates a joint problem
Yes, and the only remedy is rest
No, it only affects people who exercise
explanation: Some morning stiffness is ordinary. It typically loosens with gentle movement. Stiffness that is severe or persistent is worth asking about.

review.notes: Claim is fine but the item is guessable without knowing anything: all three distractors are absolutes ('always indicates', 'the only remedy', 'only affects people who exercise') and the key is the only hedged option, so a test-wise nine-year-old picks it by pattern. Rewrite at least two distractors as plausible non-absolute beliefs (e.g. 'Yes, and it usually means you slept badly'). Also consider naming the actual red line in the explanation — stiffness lasting more than about an hour most mornings is the thing worth asking about — rather than the vague 'severe or persistent'.

question: Why is falling treated so seriously in older adults?
options: Bones in older adults cannot heal at all
The fear afterward reduces movement
Falls are much more common than in younger people
Older adults fall from greater heights on average
explanation: The fall itself is often survivable. The loop that follows — less walking, weaker legs, worse balance — is what does the lasting damage.

review.notes: The keyed answer is wrong on the substance and the explanation understates a real danger to the exact audience. Falls are the leading cause of injury death in adults 65+; about half of fatal falls involve traumatic brain injury, and falls cause the large majority of hip fractures, which frequently end independent living. 'The fall itself is often survivable' is a minimising framing of that. Worse, distractor C ('Falls are much more common than in younger people') is simply true — roughly 1 in 4 adults 65+ falls each year — so the item has two defensible answers and keys the weaker one. If the post-fall fear cycle is the lesson worth teaching, ask about it directly ('After a fall, what often does damage even when nothing is broken?') and keep the physical injury risk in the explanation instead of waving it away.

question: Do you stop growing taller and then simply stay that height?
options: Yes, your height is fixed once growth finishes
No, most people continue growing slowly for life
No, height slowly decreases over decades
Yes, unless you do a lot of heavy lifting
explanation: The discs between the vertebrae lose a little height over many years, so most people end up slightly shorter than their peak.

review.notes: measured claim 'most people' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

question: What is the best predictor of how well somebody moves at eighty?
options: How athletic they were as a teenager
Their height and build
Whether they played sport at school
How much they moved in recent years
explanation: Recent decades matter far more than distant ones. Teenage athleticism you stopped using thirty years ago is not doing much for you now.

review.notes: Two problems. (1) Options A ('how athletic they were as a teenager') and C ('whether they played sport at school') say essentially the same thing, so a reader eliminates both on the logic that they cannot both be wrong separately — that plus the weak 'height and build' leaves one option standing. Collapse them into one and add a genuinely competing predictor. (2) 'The best predictor' is a superlative empirical claim carried by a `simplified` label with no sources; recent activity is strongly associated with late-life function but calling it the best predictor outruns what is cited. Either soften to 'which of these matters most' or attach a source.

question: You feel a sharp pain partway through a movement. What is the sensible response?
options: Stop that movement and find out why later
Finish the set and see if it settles
Switch to the other side and carry on
Push through slowly with lighter effort
explanation: Sharp is the word that matters. Dull effort is ordinary; sharp is your body naming a specific place, and it is worth listening to.

review.notes: Zero-information item: it is a Safety-category question in a children's app where the correct option is the only one that says stop and the other three all counsel continuing through sharp pain. No knowledge is required to answer. Secondary issue: 'find out why later' gives a nine-year-old no actual next step (tell an adult, get it looked at), which is the one place this item could have taught something. The sharp-vs-dull distinction in the explanation is good and should survive any rewrite.

question: What is the difference between ordinary effort and a warning sign?
options: Effort is felt in muscle, warnings only in joints
Effort builds gradually; a warning is sudden
A warning always hurts more than effort does
There is no reliable way to tell them apart
explanation: Effort arrives slowly and spreads out. A warning is usually abrupt and you can point at it. Not a perfect rule, but a useful one.

review.notes: The rule as stated in the option — 'effort builds gradually; a warning is sudden' — misses and actively miscategorises overuse injury, which is the most common way a beginner gets hurt and which builds gradually by definition. A reader applying this rule would file a slowly worsening tendon or shin pain under 'ordinary effort'. The explanation's 'not a perfect rule' hedge does not cover that specific failure; name it (pain that grows session on session, or that is still there the next day, is also a warning). Option D ('there is no reliable way to tell them apart') is a bare dismissal distractor and should be replaced.

question: Why is holding your breath during a hard effort discouraged?
options: It makes the movement harder than it needs to be
It uses up oxygen you will need afterward
It can spike pressure and leave you lightheaded
It prevents the muscle from working fully
explanation: Breath-holding under strain raises pressure sharply and some people go dizzy. Breathe out on the effort — that is the whole technique.

review.notes: Accurate on the Valsalva effect, appropriately unalarming, and the explanation gives an actionable fix (breathe out on the effort). Distractors are all things people actually believe.

question: You feel dizzy during a workout. What should happen next?
options: Drink water quickly and continue
Lie flat on the floor until it passes completely
Slow the pace but keep the session going
Sit down, and mention it to a doctor if it repeats
explanation: Sitting down handles the immediate risk. Dizziness that keeps happening is a question for a professional, not something to work around.

review.notes: Guessable by shape: the key is the longest option and the only one with two clauses, and it is the only one that mentions a doctor. Separately, distractor B is not wrong enough to be a distractor — lying down is legitimate first aid for dizziness, so a reader who knows that is penalised for knowing it. Make B clearly worse (e.g. 'lie flat and then finish the session'), and even out option lengths.

question: What does a good warm-up actually do?
options: Warms tissue and rehearses the movement
Removes any chance of injury occurring
Stretches muscles to their full length
Uses up energy that would otherwise cause cramp
explanation: Warmer tissue moves more easily and rehearsing the pattern wakes up the coordination for it. It reduces risk; it does not abolish it.

question: Is it sensible to exercise through a heavy cold?
options: Yes, sweating helps clear the illness faster
Gentle movement is fine; hard efforts can wait
Only if you take something for the symptoms first
No, any movement while ill is harmful
explanation: A short walk is usually fine. A hard session while genuinely unwell mostly buys you a longer illness, and anything chest-related deserves caution.

review.notes: Right advice, wrong reason, and the wrong line drawn. Standard guidance splits on fever and systemic symptoms (fever, body aches, deep fatigue) rather than on 'anything chest-related' — that is the above-the-neck rule, and the reason behind it is cardiac strain and impaired heat regulation while febrile, with a small myocarditis risk, not 'mostly buys you a longer illness'. That last claim is stated as fact and is not well supported. Rewrite the explanation around fever as the stop signal, and keep the chest-symptom caution as an addition rather than the whole caveat.

question: Why does footing matter more than people expect?
options: Poor footing makes muscles work inefficiently
Most movement injuries happen on soft ground
The surface usually did something unexpected
Shoes affect how much benefit you get from walking
explanation: Wet tile, a loose rug, an unseen step. The movement is rarely the problem; the ground doing something you did not predict usually is.

review.notes: Concrete, useful, and the explanation earns its place with real examples rather than restating the option.

question: What is the right amount of water to drink during ordinary activity?
options: A fixed amount measured before you start
As much as you can manage, to stay ahead of thirst
Nothing until the session is finished
Roughly what thirst asks for
explanation: For ordinary activity thirst is a decent guide. Drinking far beyond it is not safer, and in rare cases it is its own problem.

review.notes: Matches current drink-to-thirst guidance for ordinary activity and correctly declines to treat more as safer. No meal/body framing issues.

question: Somebody offers you advice about your knee. When is it worth acting on?
options: When it comes from somebody who has examined it
When several people have said the same thing
When it comes from an experienced athlete
When it matches what you read online
explanation: A joint is specific to its owner. Advice that has not met your knee is a guess, however confident or well-meant it is.

question: What is the safest way to begin after a long time away from moving?
options: At the level you managed before the gap
Below what you think you can do, for a few weeks
With the hardest session you can complete
With stretching only, until flexibility returns
explanation: Starting under your capacity is how you get to do it again tomorrow. Most restart injuries come from resuming at the old level.

review.notes: The advice is good but the explanation invents a statistic: 'most restart injuries come from resuming at the old level' is an unsourced quantified claim under a `simplified` label. This is the firmness failure the rubric calls out. Say it as the pattern it is ('a common way people get hurt on a restart is picking up where they left off') or attach a source. The option text itself is fine.

question: Why is exercising in heat treated differently?
options: Heat makes muscles more likely to tear
Sweat removes minerals the muscles need to contract
Cooling is competing with the effort for blood flow
Warm air carries less oxygen than cool air
explanation: Your body sends blood to the skin to shed heat and to the muscles to do the work. In real heat those demands compete, so the same effort costs more.

review.notes: Real mechanism, correctly explained, and it beats the folk answers without mocking them.

question: What is a reasonable way to judge whether a new movement is too much?
options: Whether it leaves you sore the next day
Whether it feels harder than last time
Whether other people find it easy
Whether you can still talk during it
explanation: The talk test is crude and surprisingly good. If you cannot get a sentence out, you are working harder than a first session needs.

review.notes: Talk test is a well-established crude intensity gauge and the explanation says so without overselling it.

question: Your knee clicks but does not hurt. What does that usually mean?
options: Painless joint noise is usually ordinary
It is a warning that pain is coming
It means the joint needs more rest
It indicates the movement is being done wrong
explanation: Joints make noise. Painless clicking is very common and usually means little. Noise that comes with pain or swelling is a different question.

review.notes: corpus gate: all three distractors start 'It', so the correct option is the odd one out by grammar. Reworded in the generator; needs re-review because the author made the change.

question: Why do instructions often say to move slowly when learning something new?
options: Slow movement uses more muscle
Speed hides mistakes you would otherwise feel
It is the only way to avoid getting out of breath
Slow movements are easier on the heart
explanation: At speed, momentum does part of the work and covers up a rough pattern. Slowing it down is how the mistake becomes noticeable.

review.notes: Explains the mechanism (momentum masking the pattern) rather than restating the option.

question: How soon after starting to move do most people notice a change in mood?
options: Only after several weeks of consistency
Usually the following day
Often within the first few minutes
Only after the activity becomes easy
explanation: The mood change tends to arrive far sooner than any physical change, which is why it is the more reliable reason to start.

review.notes: 'Often within the first few minutes' is firmer than the evidence. The acute-exercise literature generally finds mood benefit from bouts of about ten minutes upward, measured during and after the bout, and affect during effort depends on intensity — above the ventilatory threshold it typically gets worse before it gets better. A child who feels nothing at minute two and concludes it is not working is the failure mode. Rephrase to something like 'often within a single short session, not weeks' and add a source, or downgrade the timing claim.

question: Why does a walk often help when you are stuck on a problem?
options: Walking sends more oxygen to the brain
It gives you time to think without interruption
Physical effort resets your concentration
Loosening attention lets connections surface
explanation: Solutions tend to arrive when you stop gripping the problem. Walking is good at loosening the grip without emptying your head entirely.

review.notes: No single defensible right answer. Distractor B ('it gives you time to think without interruption') is at least as good an explanation as the key, and C is not far behind, so a reader who thinks about it carefully can land on B and be marked wrong. The key also asserts a cognitive mechanism ('loosening attention lets connections surface') that is a hypothesis, not a settled finding, under a `simplified` label with no sources — the walking/creativity effect is reasonably well evidenced but its mechanism is not. Either narrow the question so only one option fits, or relabel and source it.

question: What tends to happen to motivation when you wait for it before starting?
options: It usually follows the action
It builds steadily until you act
It arrives more reliably in the morning
It returns once you have rested enough
explanation: Starting is usually what produces the motivation, not the other way round. Waiting to feel like it is waiting for the wrong thing.

review.notes: Honestly labelled `editorial`; distractors are all real beliefs people hold.

question: Why is a very small daily amount often better than an occasional large one?
options: Small amounts are better for the heart
The habit survives the days you have no time
Large sessions do not count toward a habit
It is easier to recover from small sessions
explanation: A two-minute version you can do on a terrible day keeps the thread intact. An hour you can only manage sometimes breaks every time you cannot.

review.notes: Editorial and labelled as such; the explanation gives a concrete image (the two-minute version on a terrible day) rather than restating the option.

question: What does rumination — going over something repeatedly — respond to?
options: Trying harder to stop thinking about it
Analyzing it until it resolves
Doing something that occupies attention gently
Waiting for the feeling to pass on its own
explanation: Rumination needs somewhere else to go, and it does not go on command. A walk gives attention a mild job, which is often enough.

review.notes: Stated more firmly than the evidence supports, on the sample's most clinically adjacent topic, with no source. Two points: (a) 'Analyzing it until it resolves' is marked flatly wrong, but the brooding/reflection distinction is real and reflective, problem-focused processing does have support — the distractor is partly true, which makes the item misleading rather than simplified; (b) the evidence for gentle distraction is short-term relief, not that rumination 'responds to' it, and the item offers no signal that persistent rumination is worth telling someone about. At min_age 9 this reads as a settled answer to a question that is not settled.

question: Is it normal to enjoy an activity less on some days than others?
options: No, that means the activity is wrong for you
No, enjoyment should build steadily
Yes, but only when you are unwell
Yes, and it says very little about the activity
explanation: Enjoyment fluctuates for reasons that have nothing to do with the activity. A flat day is not evidence about whether it is the right thing.

review.notes: Kind, non-shaming, editorial and labelled as such.

question: What is the effect of comparing your progress to somebody else's?
options: It measures you against a starting point that is not yours
It provides a useful benchmark for your own pace
It helps most when the other person is close to your level
It reliably increases how consistent you are
explanation: You cannot see where they started, what else is in their week, or what their body does with the same work. The comparison is missing its baseline.

review.notes: The stem asks for an effect, but the keyed option states a mechanism ('measures you against a starting point that is not yours'), which is the only option not in effect-form and the only critical one among three positive ones - both tells. Worse, distractor index 2 ('helps most when the other person is close to your level') is broadly supported by social comparison research, so a knowledgeable reader is punished. Either rewrite the stem to ask what is wrong with comparison, or replace that distractor.

question: Why does breaking a long streak often feel worse than never having one?
options: The body reacts badly to a sudden stop
Losing something feels sharper than not having had it
Streaks create a physical dependency on routine
The days already done stop counting once it breaks
explanation: Losing a thing lands harder than never having it — a well-documented quirk. Worth knowing, because the days you already did still happened.

review.notes: The explanation's first sentence is a verbatim restatement of the keyed option and never names or explains the mechanism (loss aversion / the value already banked). Also 'a well-documented quirk' is firmer than warranted: loss aversion's robustness and magnitude are actively disputed (Gal & Rucker 2018, 'The Loss of Loss Aversion'). Name the effect, say why losses weigh more, and soften to 'a well-known pattern' or label the item contested.

question: What usually makes a habit stick to a particular time of day?
options: Choosing the time when you have most energy
Setting a reminder for that time each day
Attaching it to something you already do then
Picking a time nobody will interrupt
explanation: Anchoring to an existing routine — after brushing your teeth, before lunch — outperforms reminders, because the anchor is already reliable.

review.notes: 'Anchoring ... outperforms reminders' is a firm head-to-head comparative claim with confidence 'simplified' and no source. The peer-reviewed evidence does not support it that flatly - reminder and prompt interventions perform well in large behaviour-change trials, and the anchoring-beats-reminders figures in circulation come from popular blogs, not trials. Drop the comparison and just explain why an existing routine is a reliable cue, or cite a real trial.

question: How much does a single missed day matter to long-term progress?
options: It sets you back roughly a week
It undoes the adaptation you had built
It matters more the longer you have been going
It matters only if it becomes several
explanation: One day is invisible in the long run. What matters is whether it becomes the shape of the next fortnight.

review.notes: True, well-pitched, anti-shame, and the explanation adds the real idea (the pattern, not the day).

question: Why do people often underestimate how much a short walk helped?
options: They compare it to the walk they meant to take
The benefit takes hours to appear
Short walks genuinely do very little
The effect is too small to notice reliably
explanation: Ten minutes gets measured against the thirty you intended, and comes out looking like a failure instead of ten more minutes than nothing.

review.notes: Editorial framing is honestly labelled and the reference-point point is genuinely useful.

question: What is a realistic thing to expect from movement on a bad day?
options: It will resolve what is making the day bad
It will probably make the day slightly more bearable
It will make you enjoy the rest of the day
It will have no effect unless you do enough of it
explanation: Slightly more bearable is a real result and it is usually what is on offer. Expecting it to fix the day is how it ends up looking useless.

review.notes: Textbook form-tell: all four options share the frame 'It will...', and the correct one is the only hedged, non-absolute option ('will probably... slightly'). The other three are absolutes ('will resolve', 'will make you enjoy', 'will have no effect unless'). A reader who knows nothing about the topic picks the hedged option and is right. The underlying claim is true, safe and well-judged; the option set has to be rebuilt so at least two distractors are also hedged.

question: Why is it worth noticing the days you nearly skipped but did not?
options: They burn more energy than ordinary days
They indicate you are training hard enough
They are the days that prove the habit is real
They predict how long the streak will last
explanation: Anybody can do it on an easy day. The nearly-skipped ones are where the habit is actually being built.

question: What does sleep have to do with how hard a workout feels?
options: None — effort is purely physical
Poor sleep only affects long sessions
Sleep affects recovery but not the session itself
Poor sleep makes the same effort feel harder
explanation: After a poor night the same work registers as more demanding. The workout did not change; your reading of it did.

review.notes: Poor sleep raising perceived exertion at a fixed workload is solid, and the explanation adds the distinction between the work and the reading of it.

question: Why does standing on one leg get easier within a few days of practice?
options: The nervous system gets better at making corrections
The muscles grow measurably stronger that quickly
Your inner ear becomes more sensitive
Your body shifts its weight lower over time
explanation: Early gains are almost entirely the nervous system learning to correct faster and smaller. Muscle takes considerably longer.

question: What happens to your balance when you close your eyes?
options: It is unaffected if your legs are strong
It gets harder; one input of three is gone
It improves, because you concentrate harder
It only changes for people over sixty
explanation: Balance runs on vision, the inner ear and sensors in your feet and joints. Remove vision and the other two have to work considerably harder.

review.notes: Safety: the rubric bars eyes-closed movement, and this item invites a child or a senior to test it by closing their eyes while balancing with no caveat at all. Add an explicit instruction that eyes-closed balance is only done seated or with a hand on something solid. Separately, the keyed option is the only one carrying its own mini-explanation ('; one input of three is gone'), which makes it pickable on form alone - move that clause into the explanation.

question: Why is balance practice usually done near something to hold?
options: Holding on makes the practice more effective
It keeps the exercise from becoming too easy
So you can practice the harder version safely
It prevents the ankles from getting tired
explanation: A hand near a wall means you can work right at the edge of your ability, which is where balance improves, without the cost of getting it wrong.

review.notes: Good safety content, and the explanation gives the real reason (working at the edge of ability) rather than restating.

question: What is 'proprioception'?
options: The ability to balance on uneven ground
The speed at which you react to a stumble
The way the inner ear detects movement
Knowing where your limbs are
explanation: It is why you can touch your nose with your eyes shut. Joints and muscles constantly report their position, and you never notice until it fails.

review.notes: The citation is wrong. NBK556154 is 'Environmental Justice Concerns and the Proposed Atlantic Coast Pipeline Route in North Carolina' (RTI Press, 2018) - it has nothing to do with proprioception or physiology. This is the only item in the slice marked confidence 'established', and its single source does not support the claim. The claim itself is correct and the options are well built, so replace the source with a real one (e.g. StatPearls 'Physiology, Sensory System', NBK547656) and re-verify. Any other item in the library citing NBK556154 should be checked too.

question: Why does walking on sand or grass feel more tiring than pavement?
options: The surface absorbs some of each push
Soft ground is colder and drains energy
You automatically walk faster on soft ground
Uneven ground shortens your stride
explanation: Some of every step goes into moving the ground rather than you, and your ankles do extra work stabilizing. Same distance, more effort.

review.notes: Energy cost of walking on sand is 2.1-2.7x pavement and grass sits between, driven by work done deforming the substrate - the stated mechanism is right. Grass is the weaker half of the premise but not misleading.

question: What does catching yourself after a trip mostly rely on?
options: Leg strength built up over years
A correction that beats conscious thought
Having seen the obstacle in advance
Reflexes that only work when you are rested
explanation: The recovery step is underway before you are consciously aware of tripping. Deciding to catch yourself would be far too slow.

review.notes: Automatic postural responses do precede conscious awareness; explanation earns its place.

question: Why is agility trained with changes of direction rather than straight lines?
options: Straight-line movement does not build muscle
Changing direction is more tiring than running
Turning is where control gets tested
Straight lines are easier to do incorrectly
explanation: Almost nothing in ordinary life is a straight line. The moment you turn, stop or step aside is where control gets used.

review.notes: The keyed answer is near-tautological - 'turning is where control gets tested' is close to the definition of agility, so the item tests nothing. Option 0 ('straight-line movement does not build muscle') is a throwaway no reader would pick. Rework so the item teaches an actual mechanism (deceleration and re-acceleration load, changing the base of support under momentum) rather than restating the category.

question: Does balance need to be practiced for long to improve?
options: Yes, at least thirty minutes at a time
Yes, but only if done on an unstable surface
No, it improves on its own with ordinary walking
No, brief practice done often works well
explanation: A minute here and there while the kettle boils adds up better than a long session once a week. Frequency beats duration for this one.

review.notes: Short frequent balance practice is consistent with standard fall-prevention programming, and the advice is safe.

question: What makes carrying something in one hand harder than it looks?
options: Your whole body compensates for the uneven load
The arm tires faster than the legs do
One-sided loads are heavier to lift initially
It forces you to walk more slowly
explanation: Everything from your ankle to your neck adjusts to keep you upright. That is real work, which is why a one-sided carry is a genuine exercise.

review.notes: measured claim 'harder than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

question: Why do people often balance better on their non-dominant side than expected?
options: That side has naturally stronger muscles
That side gets more stabilizing practice
Balance is unrelated to which side you favor
The dominant side is usually more injured
explanation: The side you do not lead with often spends more time holding you steady while the other one acts. It quietly gets good at it.

review.notes: Both the premise and the mechanism are stated far more firmly than the evidence supports, and the item is labelled 'simplified' rather than contested. The review literature on monopedal balance and limb dominance does not reach consensus, and several studies in sedentary adults, adolescents and athletes found no significant difference between legs - which means distractor index 2 ('balance is unrelated to which side you favor') is at least as defensible as the keyed answer. Either relabel as contested and say in the text that the evidence is mixed, or cut the item.

question: Why does the same walk feel easier outside than on a treadmill?
options: Outdoor air contains more oxygen
You naturally walk more slowly outdoors
Scenery absorbs some of your attention
Treadmills require more muscular effort
explanation: Attention is part of how hard something feels. A view takes some of it, so there is less left over to spend noticing the effort.

review.notes: Attentional dissociation lowering perceived effort is sound, and the three distractors are all real misconceptions.

question: What is the main reason morning daylight is recommended?
options: It is the coolest part of the day for exercise
Morning air is cleaner in most places
Sunlight is strongest and most beneficial then
It helps set the timing of your sleep
explanation: Light in the morning is one of the strongest signals your body clock uses, and it mostly shows up that night as falling asleep more easily.

review.notes: measured claim 'most places' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

question: Why does walking uphill raise effort so much more than speeding up?
options: You are lifting your whole body against gravity
Hills require a completely different muscle group
The incline reduces how much oxygen you take in
Uphill walking uses a less efficient stride
explanation: On the flat you mostly move forward. Uphill you also move up, and raising your body weight is expensive.

review.notes: measured claim 'more than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

question: What is the sensible way to dress for exercising in the cold?
options: One heavy layer that blocks all wind
Several thin layers you can remove
As little as possible, since you warm up
Whatever keeps you warmest at the start
explanation: You will be considerably warmer ten minutes in. Layers let you shed heat rather than choosing between freezing at the start and sweating later.

review.notes: Practical, safe, and the explanation gives the reason rather than the rule.

question: Why does cold air sometimes make your chest feel tight when exercising?
options: Cold air carries less oxygen than warm air
Cold air narrows the blood vessels in the chest
Cold dry air can irritate the airways
The lungs contract slightly in cold conditions
explanation: It is usually dryness and cold irritating the airway. Breathing through a scarf warms the air first. Persistent tightness is worth asking about.

review.notes: Close, but this is a respiratory symptom in an app read by nine-year-olds, and the item leads with 'it is usually dryness', which normalises a sign that can be exercise-induced asthma. The escalation line, 'persistent tightness is worth asking about', never says who to ask. Make it concrete - tell an adult, and see a doctor if it keeps happening - and put the caveat before the reassurance rather than last.

question: What does being near trees and greenery appear to do for people?
options: It improves lung function measurably
It increases how far people walk
It has no measurable effect beyond the walking
It is associated with lower reported stress
explanation: Time in green space is consistently associated with lower stress. Exactly why is still argued over, but the association holds up well.

review.notes: Correctly hedged to association rather than cause, and the text does say what is argued over, which is what 'contested' requires. Minor construction tell: the keyed option is the only tentatively worded one among three firm claims, so a test-savvy reader can pick it on tone.

question: Why is it worth varying the route you walk?
options: New surroundings keep attention engaged
Different routes work different muscles
Repeating a route reduces its benefit
Variety is needed to keep improving fitness
explanation: The physical benefit is much the same. The difference is whether you are still noticing anything, and a familiar route stops being noticed.

review.notes: Editorial, honestly labelled, and the explanation does the work the answer option does not. Options 2 and 3 overlap enough that a test-wise reader can pair-eliminate them, but option 1 is a genuine competitor.

question: What happens to your pace when you walk with headphones on?
options: It stays the same as walking in silence
It drifts toward the rhythm you hear
It becomes much more irregular
It slows because you are distracted
explanation: People drift toward the beat without meaning to. Useful if you want to pick the pace up, and worth knowing if you meant to go gently.

review.notes: The question says 'headphones', the answer says 'the rhythm you hear' — a podcast or audiobook has no rhythm, so the stem does not support the answer. Say 'music with a steady beat' in the question. Also soften the firmness: spontaneous (uninstructed) entrainment is modest and mainly occurs when the track's tempo is already close to your natural cadence, not for any tempo you play.

question: Why is a short walk after eating often suggested?
options: It makes the meal digest completely
It prevents discomfort from eating too quickly
It helps steady the rise in blood sugar
It is the best time of day for exercise
explanation: Moving muscles take up some of the sugar from the meal, which softens the peak. Ten minutes is enough to matter.

review.notes: Claim verified and correctly hedged ('helps steady the rise'), but the option set gives it away: it is the only on-topic answer. 'It makes the meal digest completely' is nonsense, 'It prevents discomfort from eating too quickly' is a non sequitur, and 'It is the best time of day for exercise' does not answer the question asked. Also miscategorized — a postprandial glucose item is filed under 'Outdoors'.

question: What is the most common reason people skip an outdoor walk?
options: The weather being genuinely unsuitable
Not having the right clothing for it
Having nowhere pleasant nearby to walk
Deciding before looking outside
explanation: The forecast in your head is usually worse than the weather. Stepping outside first turns the decision into a real one.

review.notes: 'What is the MOST COMMON reason people skip an outdoor walk' is an empirical claim about population frequency, answered from editorial opinion with no data behind it — exactly the over-firm framing the rubric warns about. Either cite survey evidence, or rewrite the stem as a claim you can actually stand behind, e.g. 'What is a common trap when deciding whether to walk outdoors?'

question: How long does it actually take to form a habit?
options: Around two months, with huge variation
Exactly twenty-one days for most people
A fixed period that depends on the activity
Habits form immediately or not at all
explanation: The often-quoted twenty-one days has no good evidence behind it. Measured studies found an average nearer two months and a very wide spread.

review.notes: Source is Lally et al. 2010 (EJSP, doi 10.1002/ejsp.674) and it says what the item says: median 66 days, range 18-254. '21 days' is a genuinely attractive distractor, so the item is not a freebie despite being the only hedged option. Minor: explanation says 'studies' plural for one cited study.

question: What is the most useful size for a new habit?
options: Large enough to produce visible results
Small enough to do on your worst day
Whatever you can manage on a good day
The same size as the habit you want eventually
explanation: The floor matters more than the ceiling. A habit sized for your worst day is one that never has to break.

review.notes: Honestly labelled editorial, all four options are things people actually believe, and the explanation adds a reason rather than restating.

question: What tends to happen after the first missed day?
options: The habit is effectively broken
Motivation increases to compensate
Nothing, unless a second one follows
The next session feels noticeably harder
explanation: One miss changes almost nothing. Two in a row is where a habit starts becoming a thing you used to do.

review.notes: Half of this is evidence-backed and half is folklore presented as fact. Lally 2010 found a single missed opportunity did not materially affect habit formation — that part is fine. But 'two in a row is where a habit starts becoming a thing you used to do' is the 'never miss twice' rule of thumb from Atomic Habits / Tiny Habits, not a measured threshold, and it is baked into the correct option itself ('unless a second one follows'). Either drop the two-day threshold from the option and explanation, or mark it plainly as a rule of thumb rather than a finding.

question: Why is tracking something often enough to change it?
options: Tracking creates a record you can analyze
It makes the activity feel more official
It reminds you at the right time of day
Noticing a behavior tends to shift it
explanation: Simply measuring a thing nudges it, before you do anything with the numbers. Attention is part of the mechanism.

review.notes: Self-monitoring reactivity is well replicated, and the item is careful to say 'shift' rather than claiming a direction. No body or weight framing. Distractor 0 is true-but-not-an-answer, which is a good distractor rather than a bad one.

question: What is the effect of planning exactly when and where you will do something?
options: It markedly increases the chance you do it
It works only for people who like structure
It makes the plan harder to adapt later
It matters less than wanting to do it
explanation: Deciding the when and where in advance removes the moment of deliberation, and that moment is where most intentions quietly die.

review.notes: Source resolves to Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006, Adv. Exp. Soc. Psychol. 38:69-119, d = .65 across 94 independent tests. 'Markedly increases' is a fair reading of a medium-to-large effect, not an overstatement.

question: Why do habits often collapse during a change of routine?
options: Stress makes people less disciplined
The cues the habit depended on have gone
New routines take all your available energy
Habits need consistency in effort, not timing
explanation: A habit is usually held in place by its surroundings — a time, a place, a preceding event. Move house or change jobs and the scaffolding goes.

review.notes: Context-dependence of habit is solid, the simplification does not mislead, and the explanation names the mechanism (time, place, preceding event) instead of restating the option.

question: What is the best thing to do the day after missing one?
options: Do double to make up the gap
Restart the habit from the beginning
Do the ordinary session
Take a second day off to reset properly
explanation: Making up the gap treats the miss as a debt, which makes missing more costly and therefore more frightening. Just do the ordinary day.

review.notes: Stem is ungrammatical/ambiguous: 'the day after missing one' has no antecedent — missing one what? A nine-year-old reading this cold has to guess it means 'one day of the habit'. Guessability is also poor: two of three distractors ('Restart the habit from the beginning', 'Take a second day off to reset properly') are self-evidently wrong to any reader, leaving a near-binary choice. The claim itself is sound and correctly marked editorial.

question: Why is it easier to keep a habit than to start one?
options: The activity becomes physically easier over time
Motivation grows steadily once you begin
Habits become more enjoyable with repetition
Less of the decision is being made each time
explanation: A settled habit costs almost no deliberation. Starting one means paying the full decision every single time, which is the expensive part.

review.notes: Reasonable as simplified; option 2 is partly defensible but option 3 is clearly the better answer to the question as asked.

question: What does a streak actually measure?
options: How many days you turned up
How fit you have become
How much effort you have put in
How well the habit suits you
explanation: It counts turning up, and nothing else. That is a real thing worth counting, and it is worth being clear it is not a measure of fitness.

review.notes: The question cannot be got wrong. 'How many days you turned up' is the definition of a streak, and the other three options are ruled out by simply knowing what the word means — no knowledge is tested. The point being made (a streak is not a fitness measure) is worth making, but make it the thing the reader has to work out: e.g. ask what a long streak does NOT tell you, or contrast two users with the same streak and different training.

question: Why do people often overestimate what they will do next week?
options: Next week genuinely has more time in it
A future week is imagined without interruptions
Planning makes people more optimistic generally
People forget how long activities take
explanation: A week you have not lived yet has no dentist appointment or late meeting in it. Plan for the week you will actually get.

review.notes: Option 3 (people misjudge duration) is a real rival explanation rather than filler, which makes this a genuine question. Simplification is honest.

question: When does the body do most of its repair work after exercise?
options: During the session itself
In the hour immediately afterward
Largely while you are asleep
Evenly spread across the following week
explanation: Sleep is when a lot of the rebuilding happens. It is why a training plan with no sleep in it is only half a plan.

review.notes: The claim is stated more firmly than the evidence supports, and probably backwards. Measured overnight muscle protein synthesis rates are LOW — lower than daytime and lower than post-absorptive morning values unless protein is given before sleep (Res et al. 2012; Trommelen & van Loon). Post-exercise synthesis is elevated across 24-48h, not concentrated in the hours you are asleep. 'Largely while you are asleep' is a gym truism, not a finding. What IS supportable: sleep restriction impairs training adaptation and growth-hormone pulses occur in slow-wave sleep. Rewrite around 'recovery depends on sleep' rather than 'most repair happens during sleep', or reject the item.

question: Why is a rest day part of training rather than a break from it?
options: It lets you train harder the following day
It prevents boredom with the routine
It gives the mind time to recover too
The adaptation happens during the rest
explanation: Training is the signal; the change happens while you recover from it. Skip the recovery and you keep sending signals nothing acts on.

review.notes: corpus gate: all three distractors start 'It'. Same fix, same reason for re-review.

question: What is the effect of a late, hard workout on sleep?
options: It can delay sleep for some people
It reliably makes people sleep more deeply
It has no effect for anybody
It always makes falling asleep harder
explanation: It varies a lot between people. Some sleep fine; others need a couple of hours to wind down. Worth finding out which one you are.

review.notes: Two problems. (1) Guessable: three of the four options are absolutes ('reliably', 'for anybody', 'always'), so the hedged one is identifiable as correct without knowing anything about sleep. Rewrite the distractors as specific, non-absolute claims. (2) The confidence label is wrong. `contested` requires the text to say the field disagrees; this explanation describes individual variation instead. And the field is not especially divided — Stutz et al. 2019 (Sports Med) found evening exercise does not generally harm sleep, with impairment mainly after vigorous exercise ending under an hour before bed. Relabel as `simplified` and consider naming that one-hour window, which is the actually useful fact here.

question: What does 'active recovery' mean?
options: Stretching thoroughly after a hard session
Gentle movement on a day between hard efforts
Resting completely but staying on schedule
Alternating hard days with medium days
explanation: An easy walk rather than the sofa. Enough to keep blood moving and stiffness down, not enough to need recovering from.

review.notes: Definition is accurate, all four options are things the term could plausibly mean, and the explanation gives a usable test ('not enough to need recovering from').

question: Why does muscle soreness usually peak a day or two after, not immediately?
options: The muscle is still warm on the first day
Lactic acid takes that long to build up
It follows the repair, not the effort
The nervous system masks pain for the first day
explanation: The ache tracks the small-scale damage-and-repair cycle, which takes a day or so to get going. Lactic acid is long gone by then.

review.notes: Correctly kills the lactic-acid myth, which is worth the reader's attention. 'Follows the repair, not the effort' is a fair simplification of the damage-and-inflammation account, and option 3 is a genuinely tempting distractor.

question: Is soreness a sign that a workout was effective?
options: Yes, soreness is the clearest measure of progress
Yes, but only when it lasts more than a day
No, soreness always indicates something went wrong
No, it mostly reflects doing something unfamiliar
explanation: Soreness tracks novelty more than effectiveness. A good session you are used to may leave none at all.

question: What happens to reaction time and judgment after a poor night's sleep?
options: Both decline, and people usually underrate it
Both are unaffected if you feel alert
Only reaction time is affected
Both decline noticeably enough to compensate for
explanation: The awkward part is that the ability to judge your own impairment is one of the things that goes. Feeling fine is not strong evidence.

review.notes: Source is Van Dongen et al. 2003, Sleep 26(2):117-26, and it does support the specific claim that subjective alertness ratings fail to track the objective deficit. The 0-vs-3 distinction is a real one, so the item tests something.

question: Why is a consistent wake-up time often suggested over a consistent bedtime?
options: Bedtime has no effect on sleep quality
Waking is easier to control than falling asleep
Morning routines matter more than evening ones
It allows for more flexibility during the week
explanation: You cannot decide to fall asleep, but you can decide to get up. Fixing the end you control tends to pull the other end into line.

review.notes: Sensible as simplified, no sleep-hygiene overclaiming, and the explanation gives the reason (you can decide to get up, not to fall asleep) rather than restating the option.
